newsitem.title: INDIA: India adopts new higher-cost grain subsidy policy.
newsitem.headline: India adopts new higher-cost grain subsidy policy.

text.p: The Indian government on Monday announced a scheme for the sale of foodgrains to nearly 320 million people below the poverty line at cheap rates, sharply pushing up the country's food subsidy bill.
"The food subsidy bill will go up to 83 billion rupees ($2.31 billion) in 1997/98 (April-March) from 59 billion rupees in the current year," Food Minister Devendra Prasad Yadav told reporters.

Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda told parliament earlier that for people below the poverty line the government proposed to sell rice through the public distribution system (PDS) at 3.50 rupees per kg for both common and fine rice, and wheat at 2.50 rupees per kg.
Deve Gowda said that for those above the poverty line, fine rice would be sold at 6.50 rupees per kg and super fine rice at 7.50 per kg. Wheat for this category would be sold at 4.50 rupees per kg.

Rising farm subsidies have put pressure on government spending and pushed up the country's fiscal deficit. A deficit of 5.0 percent of gross domestic product is projected for the year to March 1997, against 5.9 percent in 1995/96.
Deve Gowda, a farmer turned politician, heads a 15-party alliance of regional, centrist and left-wing parties.
Soon after assuming office in June, Deve Gowda said his priorities would be rural development and to give prominence to the agriculture sector.
Yadav said the new system would be implemented in phases and by May 31 all states should be ready to put it in force.
It would be the responsibility of the state governments to identify those below the poverty line and supply them with special cards to draw foodgrains.
"The targeted public distribution system is primarily focused on the poor and will benefit 320 million people below the poverty line," Deve Gowda said in a statement.
Deve Gowda said that initially 10 kg of foodgrains would be issued every month to all families in this group.
He said the PDS operations had been widely criticised for failing to serve the population below the poverty line, its urban bias and a lack of transparent and accountable arrangements for delivery.

"The government proposes to streamline the PDS by targeting it on the poor by issuing special cards to families below the poverty line and selling essential articles under the PDS to them at specially subsidised prices," Deve Gowda said.
Yadav said about 18 million tonnes of foodgrains was likely to be issued under the targeted PDS.
Those drawing a annual income of less than 15,000 rupees had been identified as falling below the poverty line. ($1 = 35.9 rupees)
